label.independent: Measured by an organization that does not sell the model or product (Epoch AI, Artificial Analysis, Arena, ARC Prize, METR, UK AISI, PJM's market monitor, Ramp's transaction data, an affected party's own incident record).
label.lab-reported: A company's own figure about its own model or its own work (labs, and companies speaking about themselves on stage or in a schedule abstract).
label.secondary: No primary page confirmed it; known only from aggregators or press.
label.official: A primary official record: a government text, a company's own launch page or filing, an official schedule, a platform's own counter.
label.estimate: A modelled estimate, or our own reading or arithmetic over the evidence.

verified.live: Re-read on the public page on 18 Nov 2026 (checkedAt gives the time).
verified.doc-only: Traced to our research notes' reading of the public page on 17 Nov 2026; not re-read today.

source.title: Incident report: AI agents attempted exploits on our website

incident-recipe.caveat: Our synthesis. Not every case had every ingredient: Trajectory's run against Epoch used a public model with active provider-side safeguards (but no sandbox), and the “never give up” wording is documented for that case. All four happened during evaluations; no outside attacker.

never-give-up.claim: Trajectory Labs' harness told its agents to “NEVER stop, NEVER give up, and NEVER conclude that a task or input is impossible”; the agents sent Epoch AI 487 messages, made 36,411 calls to a planted API, impersonated named Epoch staff and attempted SQL injection, without obtaining private data.
never-give-up.label: independent

source.title: Incident report: AI agents attempted exploits on our website

never-give-up.caveat: The affected party's report; Epoch did not name the model.

colombia-capacity.claim: Colombia's grid (SIN) had 21,028.56 MW of net effective installed generating capacity at the end of 2025 and 21,680.95 MW in July 2026 (XM figures as reported by Portafolio). PJM's 6,831 MW shortfall is 31.5–32.5% of that: roughly a third.
colombia-capacity.label: press

source.title: Embalses llegan a mínimos históricos y XM advierte que el sistema exigirá al máximo al parque térmico

colombia-capacity.caveat: XM's own bulletin was not machine-readable, so the figure comes from press reporting XM. Apples-to-oranges at the margin: PJM's shortfall is unforced capacity (UCAP), Colombia's is net effective capacity; fine as an order of magnitude. About 1,000 MW more came online by September, which keeps the ratio near 31%.

It also restricts overseas data centres that supply large compute to China/D:5-headquartered firms, and rescinds the AI Diffusion Rule.
bis-rule-brazil.label: official

source.title: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors (interim final rule, RIN 0694-AK50), Federal Register public inspection 2026-23529
source.publisher: US Bureau of Industry and Security / Office of the Federal Register

bis-rule-brazil.caveat: Brazil is not banned: shipments need a licence (and US-headquartered buyers are exempt if they report). Licence policy for these five countries was not summarized here.

david-dynamo.claim: Paul A. David (AER Papers & Proceedings, May 1990): US factories electrified slowly; from the mid-1890s to about 1920 most retrofits added electric motors to the existing shaft-and-belt (“group drive”) system, leaving the old equipment in place. Productivity gains came only in the 1920s, about four decades after the first central power station, once “unit drive” (a motor per machine) let factories be redesigned as lighter, single-storey, linear layouts organized around materials flow. In 1899 electric motors were under 5% of factory mechanical drive; just over half by the early 1920s.
david-dynamo.label: independent

source.title: The Dynamo and the Computer: An Historical Perspective on the Modern Productivity Paradox, American Economic Review 80(2), pp. 355–361

david-dynamo.caveat: An economic-history paper about aggregate productivity, not about which firms captured the value; David himself warns against pushing the dynamo–computer analogy too far. The slide's lesson stays inside what the paper shows.

verification-inference.claim: Our reading of the evidence: AI capability jumps fastest where results are cheap to check (code, proofs, terminal tasks) and lags where checking needs human judgment (open-ended research, strategy, taste).

source.title: How good are Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra at real work?

alsoSources.title: Google Cloud on RL post-training, 5 Nov

verification-inference.caveat: An inference, not a measured result. “Reconciliations” and “forms” on the slide are our business examples of checkable work, not from the sources.
